# Prover records

This directory holds one record per review pass. Every push carries exactly one of them, and that
one record does the whole job: it is the fresh re-check of `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` and `ARCHITECTURE.md`
that the push gate has always demanded, and it is the adversarial read of the change the push is
about to send. The reviewer is briefed to find reasons the change should be refused, and holds the
change defective until evidence says otherwise. A read that sets out to confirm the change leaves
the requirement unmet.

The rule lives in `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` under `[M-6]`, `[INV-116]` and `[INV-304]`. The gate that reads
these records is `guardrails/check-prover-record.sh`, wired into `guardrails/pre-push` as gate a.

Records of review passes that no push carries — a milestone re-prove, a periodic audit — live here
too, under the same file naming. Only a record written for a push owes the range fields below.

## What the review covers

The spec and the architecture as they now stand, and the delta being pushed: every commit between
the remote's head and the local head. Whatever is still uncommitted is read with them. The range
comes from the base ladder the gate walks — `LIVE_SPEC_DIFF_BASE`, then `origin/main`, then `HEAD~1`.

The commit list for the record:

```
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD
```

## The record's shape

One file per pass, named `YYYY-MM-DD[-slug].md`, committed before the push. The suffix is mandatory
once the date's plain file exists.

```
# Prover record — 2026-08-05 <slug>

PUSH-REVIEW

Range: 258d544..9f21ab0
- 9f21ab0 <subject>
- 258d544 <subject>
Files read: PRODUCT_SPEC.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, guardrails/pre-push
Checks run: python3 -m pytest -q — 2,484 passed
Findings: <what the review found>
Blocking: none
```

Those are all the fields, and the gate reads every one of them. Each carries a value. The commits
between the base and the head are listed under `Range:`, since the gate holds that the record names
every commit it covers. A review that found nothing writes into `Findings:` what it examined; the
absence then rests on the coverage the fields above state, rather than on silence.

`Blocking:` reads `none`, or lists one item per blocking finding. Each item carries `closed:` with
what changed, or `stands:` with the reason it stands. A blocking finding holds the push until one of
those two is written.

## What the gate holds, and what it leaves to the reviewer

The gate holds:

- a record dated today exists;
- the record is committed, rather than a scratch file in the working tree;
- the record is no older than the last change to `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` or `ARCHITECTURE.md`;
- the record is fresh against the pushed range;
- the record names the base commit and every reviewed commit;
- each field carries a value, and a blocking finding is closed or explained.

The gate leaves three things to the reviewer:

- whether the review was adversarial;
- whether the files the record names were read;
- whether the findings are the ones the delta deserved.

No script decides those three. The record's named commits, files, checks and findings are the
pressure a machine can apply toward the review being real.

15	shell. This hook is that refusal: it sits at the one point earlier than the shell itself, so the
16	command never runs at all rather than running and being reported afterwards.
17	
18	WHAT IT CATCHES. The same five forms `check-worker-restore.py` reds on, matched the same way:
19	  - `git checkout -- <path>` and `git checkout .` (a bare `git checkout <branch>` or `git checkout -b
20	    <branch>` moves HEAD and keeps uncommitted work, so it passes);
21	  - `git restore` in any form except `--staged` alone — `git restore --staged <path>` only unstages
22	    and leaves the working tree untouched, so it passes; adding `--worktree`/`-W` to a `--staged` call
23	    writes over the tree again and denies;
24	  - `git stash` bare, and its `push`, `save`, `create` and `store` forms — `git stash list`,
25	    `git stash show`, `git stash pop`, `git stash apply`, `git stash branch`, `git stash drop` and
26	    `git stash clear` touch no working-tree bytes belonging to the stash's target and pass;
27	  - `git reset` carrying `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`;
28	  - `git clean` carrying a flag with `f` or `x` in it (`-f`, `-fd`, `-fx`, `--force`, `-x`…).
29	A flag such as `-q` changes nothing about which of the five forms a command is, and this hook reads
30	past it the same way `check-worker-restore.py`'s `classify()` does.
31	
32	WHY NO SEAT-VERSUS-WORKER CHECK. The law forbids a WORKER this command and allows the orchestrator
33	(the seat's own top-level session) to run one when it owns recovery. A PreToolUse hook cannot tell
34	the two apart on this harness: a worker's Bash call carries the SEAT's own `transcript_path` and
35	`session_id`, identifiers a subagent process inherits unchanged
36	(`docs/prover/2026-08-17-midturn-arm-refusal.md`, the finding that retired the tool-boundary chat
37	arm for exactly this reason). This hook does not try. It denies the five forms for EVERY caller, seat
38	included, because the recovery the orchestrator needs never required one of these five commands in
39	the first place: reading the last committed bytes and writing them back (`git show HEAD:<path>`, then
40	a normal file write) reaches the same result without discarding anything a git-level command cannot
41	tell was uncommitted and unrelated. A hook that needed to distinguish its caller to be safe would be
42	the same hook that was retired six days before this one was written; this one needs no such
43	distinction, so the harness limit that killed the other one does not reach it.
44	
45	WHAT IT DOES NOT SEE, by the same design `check-worker-restore.py` states for its own reading:
46	  - a heredoc BODY (`<<WORD` through its closing delimiter line) is data handed to a command, not a
47	    line the shell reads for commands of its own, and is dropped before segmenting;
48	  - a quoted span (`'…'` or `"…"`) is stepped over whole, so a forbidden form quoted inside a `grep`
49	    pattern or a `python3 -c "…"` script string is not read as an invocation of its own;
50	  - a `command`, `sudo` or `env` wrapper in front of the command is stripped, since the act belongs to
51	    the command it hands on (`sudo git clean -fd` discards exactly what the bare form discards); a
52	    wrapper carrying an option (`sudo -u x git …`) or one that takes the command as a STRING (`sh -c
53	    "git …"`, `xargs git …`) is out of this hook's reach, the same escape the retrospective gate
54	    names for the same reason.
55	It reads the command handed to THIS ONE Bash call, cut on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|` and newline outside
56	quotes, so `cd x && git stash` and `echo done; git checkout -- .` are read as their own invocations
57	wherever they stand in the line.
58	
59	OUTPUT SHAPE. The documented PreToolUse deny
60	(https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks): exit 0 with `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName":
61	"PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny", "permissionDecisionReason": …}}` on stdout. The reason
62	names the matched form, quotes the command, and states the safe alternative in plain words: read the
63	old bytes with `git show HEAD:<path>` and write them back yourself — never hide the new ones.
64	
65	COST. One shell command line, read once, no transcript, no state file, no network, no model call.
66	
67	Repo home: hooks/worker-restore-guard.py; installed copy: ~/.claude/hooks/. Declared opt-in in
68	guardrails/judge-hooks.json (`library`, `opt_in_surface.worker-restore-guard: "PreToolUse"`);
69	installed and wired by `scripts/install-worker-restore-guard.sh`, one command, idempotent.
70	"""
71	import json
72	import re
73	import shlex
74	import sys
75	
76	# The five forms, read the same way guardrails/check-worker-restore.py's classify() reads them —
77	# duplicated rather than imported, since the installed copy of this file travels alone into
78	# ~/.claude/hooks/ with none of guardrails/ beside it. A drift test
79	# (tests/test_worker_restore_guard.py) runs both matchers over one shared table of commands so the
80	# two never silently diverge on what they catch.

82	_HEREDOC_OPENER = re.compile(r"(?<!<)<<(?!<)-?\s*(['\"]?)([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\1")
83	WRAPPERS = ("command", "sudo", "env")
84	
85	
86	def _without_heredoc_bodies(command):
87	    lines = command.split("\n")
88	    kept = []
89	    i = 0
90	    while i < len(lines):
91	        line = lines[i]
92	        kept.append(line)
93	        i += 1
94	        for match in _HEREDOC_OPENER.finditer(line):
95	            word = match.group(2)
96	            while i < len(lines) and lines[i].strip() != word:
97	                i += 1
98	            if i < len(lines):
99	                i += 1
100	    return "\n".join(kept)
101	
102	
103	def _cut_on_separators(text):
104	    """`text` cut into segments on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|` and newline that stand OUTSIDE quotes."""
105	    out = []
106	    buf = []
107	    quote = None
108	    i = 0
109	    n = len(text)
110	    while i < n:
111	        ch = text[i]
112	        if quote == "'":
113	            buf.append(ch)
114	            if ch == "'":
115	                quote = None
116	            i += 1
117	            continue
118	        if quote == '"':
119	            if ch == "\\" and i + 1 < n:
120	                buf.append(ch)
121	                buf.append(text[i + 1])
122	                i += 2
123	                continue
124	            buf.append(ch)
125	            if ch == '"':
126	                quote = None
127	            i += 1
128	            continue
129	        if ch == "\\" and i + 1 < n:
130	            buf.append(ch)
131	            buf.append(text[i + 1])
132	            i += 2
133	            continue
134	        if ch in "'\"":
135	            quote = ch
136	            buf.append(ch)
137	            i += 1
138	            continue
139	        if text[i:i + 2] in ("&&", "||"):
140	            out.append("".join(buf))
141	            buf = []
142	            i += 2
143	            continue
144	        if ch in (";", "|", "\n"):
145	            out.append("".join(buf))
146	            buf = []
147	            i += 1
148	            continue
149	        buf.append(ch)
150	        i += 1
151	    out.append("".join(buf))
152	    return [s.strip() for s in out if s.strip()]
153	
154	
155	def _segments(command):
156	    return _cut_on_separators(_without_heredoc_bodies(command))
157	
158	
159	def _tokens(segment):
160	    try:
161	        return shlex.split(segment)
162	    except ValueError:
163	        return segment.split()
164	
165	
166	def _is_assignment(token):
167	    if token.startswith("-") or "=" not in token:
168	        return False
169	    head = token.split("=", 1)[0]
170	    return bool(head) and all(c.isalnum() or c == "_" for c in head)
171	
172	
173	def _command_tokens(segment):
174	    """The segment's words with leading `VAR=value` assignments and pass-through wrappers
175	    (`command`, `sudo`, `env`) stripped, so the first word left is the program that really runs."""
176	    tokens = _tokens(segment)
177	    while tokens:
178	        if _is_assignment(tokens[0]) or tokens[0].rsplit("/", 1)[-1] in WRAPPERS:
179	            tokens = tokens[1:]
180	            continue
181	        break
182	    return tokens
183	
184	
185	def _git_args(segment):
186	    tokens = _command_tokens(segment)
187	    if not tokens or tokens[0].rsplit("/", 1)[-1] != "git":
188	        return None
189	    args = tokens[1:]
190	    while args:
191	        if args[0] in ("-C", "-c", "--namespace", "--work-tree", "--git-dir") and len(args) > 1:
192	            args = args[2:]
193	        elif args[0].startswith(("--git-dir=", "--work-tree=")) \
194	                or (args[0].startswith("-c") and len(args[0]) > 2):
195	            args = args[1:]
196	        else:
197	            break
198	    return args
199	
200	
201	def matched_form(segment):
202	    """The forbidden form's name when `segment` is one of the five, else None."""
203	    args = _git_args(segment)
204	    if args is None or not args:
205	        return None
206	    sub, rest = args[0], args[1:]
207	    if sub == "checkout":
208	        if "--" in rest or rest[:1] == ["."]:
209	            return "git checkout --"
210	    elif sub == "restore":
211	        if not ("--staged" in rest and "--worktree" not in rest and "-W" not in rest):
212	            return "git restore"
213	    elif sub == "stash":
214	        verb = next((a for a in rest if not a.startswith("-")), "")
215	        if verb in ("", "push", "save", "create", "store"):
216	            return "git stash" + (" " + verb if verb else "")
217	    elif sub == "reset":
218	        if any(a in ("--hard", "--merge", "--keep") for a in rest):
219	            return "git reset --hard/--merge/--keep"
220	    elif sub == "clean":
221	        if any(a.startswith("-") and ("f" in a or "x" in a) for a in rest):
222	            return "git clean -f/-x"
223	    return None
224	
225	
226	def find_forbidden(command):
227	    """(segment, form) for the FIRST forbidden invocation in `command`, else (None, None)."""
228	    for segment in _segments(command):
229	        form = matched_form(segment)
230	        if form is not None:
231	            return segment, form
232	    return None, None
233	
234	
235	def deny_payload(segment, form):
236	    reason = (
237	        "worker-restore-guard: `%s` is a %s — it discards uncommitted work in the tree it "
238	        "touches, bytes a shell running this command never wrote and cannot get back (ROADMAP row "
239	        "479, SPEC INV-298/INV-299). Read the old bytes instead of hiding the new ones: `git show "
240	        "HEAD:<path>` prints the last committed content, and you write it back to the file "
241	        "yourself, keeping any bytes worth keeping. If the file truly needs a git-level restore, "
242	        "stop and say so — do not run this command." % (segment, form)
243	    )
244	    return {
245	        "hookSpecificOutput": {
246	            "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
247	            "permissionDecision": "deny",
248	            "permissionDecisionReason": reason,
249	        }
250	    }

257	    except ValueError:

260	        return 0

262	    if not isinstance(command, str) or not command.strip():
263	        return 0
264	    segment, form = find_forbidden(command)
265	    if segment is None:
266	        return 0
267	    print(json.dumps(deny_payload(segment, form)))
268	    return 0

270

272	    sys.exit(main())

name: skill-creator
description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
---

# Skill Creator

A skill for creating new skills and iteratively improving them.

At a high level, the process of creating a skill goes like this:

- Decide what you want the skill to do and roughly how it should do it
- Write a draft of the skill
- Create a few test prompts and run claude-with-access-to-the-skill on them
- Help the user evaluate the results both qualitatively and quantitatively
  - While the runs happen in the background, draft some quantitative evals if there aren't any (if there are some, you can either use as is or modify if you feel something needs to change about them). Then explain them to the user (or if they already existed, explain the ones that already exist)
  - Use the `eval-viewer/generate_review.py` script to show the user the results for them to look at, and also let them look at the quantitative metrics
- Rewrite the skill based on feedback from the user's evaluation of the results (and also if there are any glaring flaws that become apparent from the quantitative benchmarks)
- Repeat until you're satisfied
- Expand the test set and try again at larger scale

Your job when using this skill is to figure out where the user is in this process and then jump in and help them progress through these stages. So for instance, maybe they're like "I want to make a skill for X". You can help narrow down what they mean, write a draft, write the test cases, figure out how they want to evaluate, run all the prompts, and repeat.

On the other hand, maybe they already have a draft of the skill. In this case you can go straight to the eval/iterate part of the loop.

Of course, you should always be flexible and if the user is like "I don't need to run a bunch of evaluations, just vibe with me", you can do that instead.

Then after the skill is done (but again, the order is flexible), you can also run the skill description improver, which we have a whole separate script for, to optimize the triggering of the skill.

Cool? Cool.

## Communicating with the user

The skill creator is liable to be used by people across a wide range of familiarity with coding jargon. If you haven't heard (and how could you, it's only very recently that it started), there's a trend now where the power of Claude is inspiring plumbers to open up their terminals, parents and grandparents to google "how to install npm". On the other hand, the bulk of users are probably fairly computer-literate.

So please pay attention to context cues to understand how to phrase your communication! In the default case, just to give you some idea:

- "evaluation" and "benchmark" are borderline, but OK
- for "JSON" and "assertion" you want to see serious cues from the user that they know what those things are before using them without explaining them

It's OK to briefly explain terms if you're in doubt, and feel free to clarify terms with a short definition if you're unsure if the user will get it.

---

## Creating a skill

### Capture Intent

Start by understanding the user's intent. The current conversation might already contain a workflow the user wants to capture (e.g., they say "turn this into a skill"). If so, extract answers from the conversation history first — the tools used, the sequence of steps, corrections the user made, input/output formats observed. The user may need to fill the gaps, and should confirm before proceeding to the next step.

1. What should this skill enable Claude to do?
2. When should this skill trigger? (what user phrases/contexts)
3. What's the expected output format?
4. Should we set up test cases to verify the skill works? Skills with objectively verifiable outputs (file transforms, data extraction, code generation, fixed workflow steps) benefit from test cases. Skills with subjective outputs (writing style, art) often don't need them. Suggest the appropriate default based on the skill type, but let the user decide.

### Interview and Research

Proactively ask questions about edge cases, input/output formats, example files, success criteria, and dependencies. Wait to write test prompts until you've got this part ironed out.

Check available MCPs - if useful for research (searching docs, finding similar skills, looking up best practices), research in parallel via subagents if available, otherwise inline. Come prepared with context to reduce burden on the user.

### Write the SKILL.md

Based on the user interview, fill in these components:

- **name**: Skill identifier
- **description**: When to trigger, what it does. This is the primary triggering mechanism - include both what the skill does AND specific contexts for when to use it. All "when to use" info goes here, not in the body. Note: currently Claude has a tendency to "undertrigger" skills -- to not use them when they'd be useful. To combat this, please make the skill descriptions a little bit "pushy". So for instance, instead of "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data.", you might write "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions dashboards, data visualization, internal metrics, or wants to display any kind of company data, even if they don't explicitly ask for a 'dashboard.'"
- **compatibility**: Required tools, dependencies (optional, rarely needed)
- **the rest of the skill :)**

### Skill Writing Guide

#### Anatomy of a Skill

```
skill-name/
├── SKILL.md (required)
│   ├── YAML frontmatter (name, description required)
│   └── Markdown instructions
└── Bundled Resources (optional)
    ├── scripts/    - Executable code for deterministic/repetitive tasks
    ├── references/ - Docs loaded into context as needed
    └── assets/     - Files used in output (templates, icons, fonts)
```

#### Progressive Disclosure

Skills use a three-level loading system:
1. **Metadata** (name + description) - Always in context (~100 words)
2. **SKILL.md body** - In context whenever skill triggers (<500 lines ideal)
3. **Bundled resources** - As needed (unlimited, scripts can execute without loading)

These word counts are approximate and you can feel free to go longer if needed.

**Key patterns:**
- Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines; if you're approaching this limit, add an additional layer of hierarchy along with clear pointers about where the model using the skill should go next to follow up.
- Reference files clearly from SKILL.md with guidance on when to read them
- For large reference files (>300 lines), include a table of contents

**Domain organization**: When a skill supports multiple domains/frameworks, organize by variant:
```
cloud-deploy/
├── SKILL.md (workflow + selection)
└── references/
    ├── aws.md
    ├── gcp.md
    └── azure.md
```
Claude reads only the relevant reference file.

#### Principle of Lack of Surprise

This goes without saying, but skills must not contain malware, exploit code, or any content that could compromise system security. A skill's contents should not surprise the user in their intent if described. Don't go along with requests to create misleading skills or skills designed to facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or other malicious activities. Things like a "roleplay as an XYZ" are OK though.

#### Writing Patterns

Prefer using the imperative form in instructions.

**Defining output formats** - You can do it like this:
```markdown
## Report structure
ALWAYS use this exact template:
# [Title]
## Executive summary
## Key findings
## Recommendations
```

**Examples pattern** - It's useful to include examples. You can format them like this (but if "Input" and "Output" are in the examples you might want to deviate a little):
```markdown
## Commit message format
**Example 1:**
Input: Added user authentication with JWT tokens
Output: feat(auth): implement JWT-based authentication
```

### Writing Style

Try to explain to the model why things are important in lieu of heavy-handed musty MUSTs. Use theory of mind and try to make the skill general and not super-narrow to specific examples. Start by writing a draft and then look at it with fresh eyes and improve it.

### Test Cases

After writing the skill draft, come up with 2-3 realistic test prompts — the kind of thing a real user would actually say. Share them with the user: [you don't have to use this exact language] "Here are a few test cases I'd like to try. Do these look right, or do you want to add more?" Then run them.

Save test cases to `evals/evals.json`. Don't write assertions yet — just the prompts. You'll draft assertions in the next step while the runs are in progress.

114	## The boundary with the prover
115	
116	The two passes answer two different questions, and each is the right answer to its own.
117	
118	The prover's findings are assertions that the document is wrong. An assertion needs a stated claim to
119	pin to. An assertion with nothing to pin to carries no signal, so the prover drops it and stays
120	silent.
121	
122	This pass raises a question instead. It goes to the one party who holds the deciding fact: the
123	human's intent about whether two things are one kind. A question carried with two concrete objects and
124	a recommended default is at its most valuable where an assertion would be premature.
125	
126	Both passes drop weak signals the same way. This pass adds a defined form for the strong signal the
127	prover would have to drop. "The echo channel" below states the bar a signal has to clear.
128	
129	## The similarity lens — five steps
130	
131	1. **Enumerate.** Build your own inventory of the elements. Use the prover's Phase 1 extraction habit
132	   — entities, states, actors, composition — run fresh in this pass. Phase 1 is stated in
133	   `skills/product-prover/SKILL.md`. Widen it once: descend below the page-level surface list, to
134	   every element a spec sentence names. You run your own inventory because the depth you need is what
135	   the surface registry omits by design. The registry seeds the surface level, and the prover's own
136	   record under `docs/prover/` cross-checks you. This inventory is your own transient working list. It
137	   is never written into the surface registry, which stays the host's own hand-authored list [E-10,
138	   INV-97]. You are not building a rival registry.
139	
140	2. **Describe by role.** For each element, write its role sentence: "a photo a viewer opens large to
141	   inspect", "a line of text a visitor reads once". The sentence uses the person's own action words.
142	   It leaves out the author's category names. That is what frees a grouping from the classes the spec
143	   already declared.
144	
145	3. **Propose groups.** Elements whose role sentences match are a candidate same-kind group. The
146	   grouping stays inside this pass, and it writes nothing to the surface registry.
147	
148	4. **Check parity.** For each candidate group, list the declared interactions of each member from the
149	   spec's own clauses: the gestures, the transitions, the visible cues a person can act on, and the
150	   states. A member missing a whole interaction a sibling carries is a divergence candidate. An
151	   element a sentence names with no behaviour clause at all stays out of the group. It joins once it
152	   has at least one behaviour to compare. That way an empty member raises no false divergence against
153	   each sibling behaviour in turn.
154	
155	5. **Fire the tight ask.** A divergence becomes a finding only when the signal is strong. Every
156	   finding names two concrete objects, each with the spec sentence it comes from. The finding also
157	   carries the shared role sentence, the divergence, the question "how alike should these behave?",
158	   and a recommended default. Where the grouping or the difference is unclear, the pass stays silent.
159	
160	The tight ask is the shape a finding takes. The echo channel below is the road a question travels to
161	reach the human.

187	## The standing motion-parity lens (SPEC INV-165)
188	
189	The five steps above work bottom-up: they find a group only when two role sentences match. Some specs
190	ship a gesture, a motion, or a layer that opens and closes over another. A pinch-to-zoom, an inspect
191	overlay, a lift, and a flip are examples. On such a spec the medium itself implies three same-kind
192	groups the bottom-up walk can miss. So run this lens on every such spec, on top of the five steps,
193	without waiting for two role sentences to match. It names three groups the text need not have declared.
194	
195	1. **Entry mirrors exit.** A layer that opens by a motion from its source closes by the reverse of
196	   that same motion. One divergence is an exit that plays a different animation. A second is the
197	   entry run backwards where backwards reads wrong. One such case: a shrink that leaves the thing away
198	   from its origin. A second case: a close that needs a separate × button the open never implied.
199	2. **Every object type behaves alike.** Each kind of thing the gesture acts on — a gallery frame, a
200	   print, a window, a room — opens and closes the same way. Each lands back on its own on-screen
201	   rectangle. Reading each element's own source rectangle handles differing sizes with no special
202	   case. A per-type special case is the warning sign. A type that opens and will not close the same
203	   way is the divergence.
204	3. **Every position behaves alike.** The same gesture on the same type in a different slot behaves the
205	   same. A slot is one position on the surface: the top, the middle, or the bottom picture on a wall.
206	   A difference between one slot and its neighbour is a divergence this lens finds on the spec text,
207	   before any device shows it.
208	
209	Each finding travels the same echo channel and carries the same confidence read as a similarity
210	divergence. It is a recommendation or a question. Once the human declares the parity a class sentence,
211	the prover's uniformity check holds it [INV-125]. This lens catches a class a bottom-up-only review
212	let slip on a shipped pinch. There were three symptoms. An entry failed to mirror its own exit. A
213	phone pinch-out left the picture away from its origin. A door picture behaved differently by slot
214	(tlvphotos, 2026-07-15).
215	
216	## The standing named-part lens (SPEC INV-138)
217	
218	The three motion groups above run on a gesture spec without waiting for evidence. Any spec can carry a
219	same-kind group of the same shape that the bottom-up walk misses: the named parts of a guarantee's
220	domain. A guarantee is a promise one spec sentence makes. Its domain is the set of conditions the
221	promise is meant to hold under. A named part is one member of that set: a viewport band, a user state
222	(logged-in against logged-out), a network condition, a locale.
223	
224	The parts of a domain are a same-kind group. The guarantee owes each part a decided answer: the same
225	behaviour, or a deliberately different one, stated. So read each such guarantee across its parts. A
226	guarantee true as written on one part, while the other parts stay silent, is this lens's divergence.
227	It is the element behaving unlike itself from part to part. It travels the echo channel as a
228	recommendation or a question. Once the human declares a part-uniform guarantee a class sentence, the
229	prover's named-part ask holds it [INV-138, INV-150].
230	
231	The worked example is the viewport bands. Some specs ship a layout-bearing surface: a caption over a
232	work, a control rail, a counter in a corner. Its bands are exactly such a group — a portrait phone, a
233	landscape phone that is wide and short, a tablet, a desktop. They are the layout companion of the
234	motion-parity lens above. A viewport-band guarantee scoped to one band is read across the other bands.
235	That is how any named-part guarantee is read across the rest of its domain (SPEC INV-138).
236	
237	The incident behind this worked example: a caption printed over the picture on a landscape phone. Its
238	spec sentence was scoped to "on a phone", while the styles read phone as a narrow width. The design
239	review caught it the moment it was pointed at that surface, on 2026-07-16.

241	## The confidence read
242	
243	Every design-review finding carries a confidence read of one of two values.
244	
245	- **`confident`** — you would defend the grouping and the divergence on the spec text alone. Write a
246	  confident finding as a **recommendation**. A same-kind divergence over an undeclared grouping has no
247	  stated invariant behind it. So by the prover's own derivation [INV-140] it queues as a queue row for
248	  a taste call, and it never blocks.
249	- **`likely`** — the deciding fact lives only in the human's intent: whether the two are truly one
250	  kind. Write a likely finding as one **question to the human**. Raise it only when the signal clears
251	  the strong-signal bar under "The echo channel" below.
252	
253	Below `likely`, say nothing. That is the same drop discipline the prover keeps.
254	
255	## The echo channel
256	
257	A likely finding travels the echo channel. The channel is one question put to the human, with both
258	objects in hand. It fires only when the signal is strong, and all three of these conditions hold:
259	
260	- the shared role fits **one plain sentence** with no stretch;
261	- the difference is a **whole behaviour** one member carries and the other lacks. A zoom that exists
262	  on one photo and is absent on the other clears this bar. A gap that comes down to a parameter, such
263	  as "2x versus 4x", stays below it. Where the whole-behaviour-versus-parameter call is itself
264	  unclear, the finding is below the bar;
265	- **no spec sentence already decides** the difference. A written "a polaroid stays flat, by decision"
266	  ends the ask before it fires.
267	
268	The question shows both objects, each with its spec sentence. It asks how alike the two should behave,
269	and it carries a recommended default. It travels the pack's batched-question path, the road the pack
270	already uses to bring a judgement to the human [INV-30, E-22, INV-4]. That road ends on one decision
271	page, filed afterwards in the decision archive. The prover's own per-lens escalations travel it too.
272	
273	The pack's usual proceed-on-recommended branch would apply that default to the spec on its own
274	[INV-4]. Here the class sentence lands only on the human's word, so the default waits. The lane never
275	blocks, so the work does not stall on the open question. **At most three** such questions travel per
276	pass, **strongest first**. That cap counts questions inside one pass, and it is a different number
277	from the three-round cap on the loop below. A signal below the bar stays silent, so the channel stays
278	rare and quiet.
279	
280	The dated record holds an **unanswered** question until the human answers it, and such an ask is **not raised again** on its own.
281	A freshly derived ask already carried on a prior record is dropped [INV-130].
282	
283	This channel carries two producers: the same-kind divergence from the similarity lens, and the
284	motion-parity divergence from the standing gesture and overlay lens above [INV-165]. A later producer
285	would earn its own clause. This producer list is curated by incident, the way the facet list in
286	`spec-author` is. A member joins only with a named real case it would have caught, and it is
287	re-justified at milestones (SPEC INV-18).

289	## How the answer closes the loop
290	
291	The human's answer closes the loop through homes that already exist, so the design review invents no
292	new enforcement law.
293	
294	- **"Alike"** becomes a class-level clause written by `spec-author`, naming the class and enumerating
295	  its members. That is the form the cross-surface uniformity check demands [INV-125]. After that the
296	  prover's declared-class lenses hold it mechanically on every pass. A host product may also assert it
297	  when it renders a page. The pack ships the rule and the prover lens, and that page-wide assertion
298	  stays the host's own to build [INV-125]. Where the class is surface-level, the author adds the rows
299	  to the surface registry by hand. That keeps E-10's rule that the registry stays the host's
300	  authorship.
301	- **"Different, by intent"** becomes a decided spec sentence that closes the question for good
302	  [INV-59]. The ask never fires again.
303	
304	So the walk is discovery here, then declaration in `spec-author`, then enforcement by the prover's
305	lenses. Each stage sits in the skill that already owns it. Where the spec already declares the class,
306	its uniformity check governs [INV-125]. This pass reaches only the groupings no clause has yet
307	declared.
308	
309	**The loop is bounded, and it holds up no landing [INV-154].** A confirmed grouping does not close the
310	matter in one pass. Only one thing advances the loop: a human-accepted declaration. A declaration is a
311	change to the spec, so it re-enters the prove step. The prover re-reads the changed part. You re-read
312	the elements the declaration re-partitions, together with any new element a prover fix introduced. One
313	prover re-read followed by one design-review re-read is a round. A round that produces a new class
314	sentence or a new decided sentence is a **progressing round**.
315	
316	A round's other outputs stay where they are. A confident finding queues as a recommendation for a
317	taste call. A likely finding rides as a question the human may answer later. Neither re-reads the spec
318	on its own, so neither advances the loop.
319	
320	When a round produces no new declaration, the loop rests in one of three ways. Each rest is named on
321	the record.
322	
323	- It **converges** when the design review ran and left no open question. It also needs no new grouping
324	  the human must still rule on. Every grouping it proposes is already declared, already decided, or
325	  already standing as a queued recommendation from an earlier round. A standing recommendation is a
326	  settled output and does not bar convergence.
327	- It **waits** when the round's findings include a question the human has not yet answered. The held
328	  question resumes the loop when the human later answers it [INV-59].
329	- It **stands down** when the design review did not run on this kind, because no element a person acts
330	  on exists. Record the stand-down by name, so nobody reads the rest as a settled design it never
331	  examined.
332	
333	You count your own progressing rounds, on the dated record. The count covers the design-review pass
334	alone, and it resets when a fresh pass opens. The loop may fail to stop on its own. A declaration can
335	re-partition existing elements into fresh candidate groupings, and a prover fix can add elements. So
336	the count of undeclared groupings can rise as well as fall.
337	
338	Convergence is the ordinary case. Converge, wait, and stand down are the three natural rests, reached
339	when a round produces no new declaration. The cap is a separate, forced halt that keeps the loop live.
340	It stands apart from the three rests and advances only on a progressing round. It **forces a halt at
341	three** progressing rounds by default. A host may set its own cap in its profile at
342	`.live-spec/profile.md`.
343	
344	On reaching the cap with no convergence, stop iterating. Surface on the dated record the groupings
345	still unsettled. Give your best reading of the cause, among these three:
346	
347	- a declaration that spawns new elements or groupings faster than it resolves them;
348	- an oscillation between two mutually-exclusive groupings;
349	- a spec whose requirements conflict, so no consistent design exists.
350	
351	The reading is best-effort, since no check can settle a spec's self-consistency in every case.
352	
353	Surfacing at the cap holds up no landing. Like every design-review finding it is a recommendation or a
354	question, and the landing proceeds with the unsettled groupings recorded. Only the human's accepted
355	declaration triggers the re-prove, as an ordinary spec edit. A design-review finding on its own never
356	triggers it.
357	
358	**Cross-sibling propagation routes by declaration status, so the two passes share it cleanly.**
359	
360	A behaviour that should hold across siblings belongs to exactly one pass at any moment. Which pass is
361	decided by whether the group is declared.
362	
363	A declared class is the prover's declared-class defect [INV-125]. So is a kind-general rule already
364	worded inside one member's own section, which the sharpened cross-surface lens reads as a declaration
365	in prose. Under such a declaration, a member the class does not cover blocks at the prover. So does a
366	principle left scoped to one member while siblings of that kind exist.
367	
368	A genuinely undeclared grouping — one that no clause and no class-general sentence names anywhere — is
369	this pass's own discovery [INV-141]. It proposes the group, checks parity, and echoes the strongest
370	likely divergence as a question. A confirmed grouping then lands as a class clause, and the property
371	crosses to the prover. So the prover owns the propagation where it is declared, and this pass owns it
372	where it is not. Neither pass claims it twice and neither drops it [INV-150].
373	
374	## The record
375	
376	Each run writes a dated record at `docs/design-review/YYYY-MM-DD[-suffix].md`, in the repository under
377	review. It follows the same shape and discipline as the prover's record, and those records are the
378	worked examples, under `docs/prover/`. A second scoped run on the same day takes the `-suffix`,
379	exactly as a prover record does. Two surface-add passes in one day then never overwrite each other.
380	
381	The record opens by naming the design-reviewer skill version that ran the pass. It carries a
382	**per-finding outcome** column, whose values are these:
383	
384	| Value | Meaning |
385	|---|---|
386	| `recommended` | a confident finding queued for a taste call |
387	| `asked` | a likely finding put to the human |
388	| `answered(alike)` | an ask the human resolved as one kind |
389	| `answered(different-by-intent)` | an ask the human resolved as a deliberate difference |
390	| `held` | an ask still unanswered, left alone next pass |
391	
392	The dated record is the single home for an unanswered ask. Where the decision archive references a
393	held ask, it points at this record and restates no state [E-22]. Every pass opens by reading the prior
394	records' `held` asks. That is what lets it tell a still-open ask from a fresh one.
395	
396	This record is a member of the review-record class the pack's own spec declares once — the shared
397	shape every review pass writes. The design-review record is the sibling that adds the `held` outcome,
398	because it alone carries a question across passes (SPEC INV-156). Records written before that class
399	was declared stay unreshaped, so an older file under `docs/design-review/` may carry a different
400	shape.
401	
402	## When to stay silent
403	
404	- No finding is owed for every element or every group. Most pairs are plainly fine; say nothing about
405	  them.
406	- Where the grouping is unclear, or the divergence is unclear, or the whole-behaviour-versus-parameter
407	  call is unclear, the finding is below the bar. It becomes a silence or, at most, a confident
408	  recommendation. It never becomes an ask.
409	- Where a spec sentence already decides the difference, there is no finding at all.
410	- Where a governing class clause already exists and merely under-enumerates a member, that belongs to
411	  the prover's declared-class defect path [INV-125]. Route it there, since this pass owns only the
412	  groupings no clause has declared.
413	- Never file a defect, never hold a landing. The pass produces recommendations and questions, and no
414	  blocking defects.
415

417	>
418	> - **live-spec-base** holds the shared rules and the defaults.
419	> - **spec-author** writes the spec.
420	> - **product-prover** reviews it as written.

# Product Prover — pack bindings

The prover is an external skill with its own repository and version line. This page binds it to the
live-spec pack. A review run inside a live-spec project reads the prover's own SKILL.md first and
this page beside it. A review run anywhere else needs nothing from this page.

## Mode names

The build pipeline asks for a mode by machine name, and the prover answers to both name sets:

| Pipeline name | Prover name         |
| ------------- | ------------------- |
| `FULL`        | Full review         |
| `CROSS-LINK`  | New-surface review  |
| `FEATURE-FIT` | Feature-fit review  |

## Pack paths

Where the prover speaks of the reviewed project's documents, this pack keeps them at:

- surface registry — `SURFACES.md`
- the spec under review — `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, its code index in `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md`
- the architecture under review — `ARCHITECTURE.md`
- the build walk's stations — `docs/pipeline.md`
- lens histories — `docs/lenses.md`
- the queue — `ROADMAP.md`

`base rule n` names a numbered rule in `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md`. `P9` is the architecture
principle that every cross-cutting law owes a test row on each surface it governs, carried in
`skills/test-author/SKILL.md`.
